title: Chapter 3 – Five Dim Lights
html:
The scan of his sister costs Lin Jian a whole morning of sleep, and it tells him almost nothing.

```
[Scan: Human Infant (Lin Yue)]
Energy channels: present, structurally complete
Channel state: sealed
Spiritual root: absent
Root structure cannot be analyzed without a reference sample.
Creation Energy +3 (24 / 100)
```

Sealed channels. No root. And no way to understand why until he has seen a root properly, from the inside, which he cannot do with any of the cultivators in the house without their feeling it. A scan is a touch of something cold, and a cultivator's skin notices cold.

That night, lying in the dark beside his sleeping brother, he makes a list. He has always made lists. In his first life they lived on whiteboards. Here they live in his head, where no one can read them.

One: learn this world.

Two: open my own channels. Get Qi.

Three: fix Father.

Four: save the vein.

He lies awake a long time. Then he adds a fifth line, more carefully than the others, as if it might break.

Five: Lin Yue gets a root.

\ \ \*

Three years is a long time to be a child when you are not one.

He spends it the way he spent his first doctorate: reading everything, watching everything, and saying very little.

By four he can read. Not officially. Officially he is learning his first fifty characters at the kitchen table with Old Nan, the stooped servant who looks after the younger children. Unofficially he has been reading the family library since the winter he learned to climb the shelves, starting with Notes on a Hundred Common Herbs and working outward. It is a narrow room at the back of the main hall, and almost no one goes there except Second Uncle, who keeps his old account books on the bottom shelf, and Grandfather, who comes at night with a lamp and reads nothing at all, only sits.

By five he has a map of the household in his head as detailed as any building plan he ever drew. Who rises first. Who cultivates where. Who drinks. Who lies.

Father rises before dawn and draws talismans until his hand gives out, then eats breakfast with his left hand tucked into his sleeve so no one will see it shaking. The yellow slips he makes come in a dozen kinds. Fire Starters for the kitchen hearths and the village ovens, which crumble into blue flame at a word. Water-gathering slips for Third Aunt's herb beds. Light charms for the hall, which the village headman buys by the dozen for his son's wedding. Mirror Guard talismans, which the clan sells to merchants traveling the Willow Ford road: tear one, and a shell of pale gold light blooms around you for the space of a few breaths, enough to turn a wolf's jaws or a bandit's knife. And Flame-Burst talismans, which are the only weapons the Lin shop sells, and which sell badly, because Father loses six in every ten before they are finished.

Third Aunt Wenqing rises at the same hour and walks the terraces with her slips and her baskets. By midmorning she is in the pill room behind the kitchen, sweating over a bronze cauldron as old as the house, rolling dark brown Breath-Gathering Pills between her palms. She gives one to each of the young cultivators every tenth day. Lin Feng swallows his without chewing. He says they taste like burnt bark. Lin Jian, who once licks one when no one is looking, privately agrees, and his panel agrees with both of them.

```
[Scan: Breath-Gathering Pill (Grade 1)]
Active fraction: 31%
Remainder: carbonized plant matter, ash, bound impurities
Note: Active compounds degraded by uneven heating.
Creation Energy +2
```

Thirty-one percent. Two-thirds of every pill the family can afford is charcoal.

Fourth Uncle Wenshi drills the village guard every morning now, not every second morning, and the men have learned to raise their arm-guard barriers in a single breath. Lin Feng trains with them twice a week, a borrowed spear in his hands, and by eleven he is better with it than any of them. By twelve he has reached the fourth layer of Qi Refining, and he has learned his first true spell, a ring of fire that spins out from his feet as he moves, scorching the packed earth in a perfect circle. Phoenix Ash Step, Uncle Mao calls it. Lin Feng is very proud of it. He sets the gate yard on fire twice.

And Uncle Mao teaches. Three mornings a week, in the courtyard below the main hall, the gray-bearded cousin from the side branch sits on a stone bench with his bad leg stretched out in front of him and teaches whichever children of the clan have tested with a root: the Green Pine Breathing Method, the names of the channels, the five elements and how they feed and break one another. Lin Jian, who has no root yet that anyone knows of, is not invited.

He listens from the eaves.

There is a place above the courtyard where the roof of the storehouse meets the wall of the main hall, a hollow in the tiles just big enough for a small boy and a twist of candied ginger. He finds it at four. He is there every lesson for two years.

"Water feeds wood," Uncle Mao says to the upturned faces below. "Wood feeds fire. Fire makes earth, the ash, you see. Earth bears metal. Metal carries water, as a cold blade gathers dew. That is the generating cycle. Learn it. Then learn the other one, the breaking cycle, because that is the one that will kill you in a fight. Water drowns fire. Fire melts metal. Metal cuts wood. Wood breaks earth. Earth dams water." He raps his cane on the stones. "Lin Hu. What drowns fire?"

"Water, Uncle," says Lin Hu, who tested at six with a fire and wood root and has been unbearable ever since.

"Good. And what does that tell you about fighting your cousin Lin Feng?"

Lin Hu does not answer. Lin Feng smiles, for the first time all morning.

"And roots," Uncle Mao says, rapping the cane for attention. "Count the elements in you. One is a heavenly root, once in a thousand years. Two is rare, and the sects send carriages for it. Three is gifted, which is what your cousin Feng has. Four and five are the common run, which is most of us and nearly every outer disciple in the Sect. The fewer the elements, the purer the Qi, and the faster it gathers. The more, the slower, because each must be refined on its own, and they quarrel in the channel." He lifts a finger. "But hear this, all of you. A five-element root has every element in it. Every art can be cast by such a cultivator, once he has the Qi to feed it. And a cultivator who lacks the element can still cast it, after a fashion, at half the strength and twice the labor. Do not let anyone tell you the many-rooted can do nothing. They can do everything. Slowly."

Above them, Lin Jian chews his ginger and thinks: It is not a cycle. It is a description of resonance. Each element's Qi vibrates in a way that strengthens the next one in the sequence and interferes with the one across from it. The old cultivators observed the pattern for ten thousand years without ever seeing the wave beneath it.

He thinks a great deal about waves in those two years.

Nobody senses him up there, and he does not wonder why until later. A cultivator's sense finds Qi. A small boy with none gives it nothing to find; to every sense in the courtyard he is a stone in the wall. It will stop being true the day he has any.

Some lessons he remembers word for word. One spring morning, when Lin Bo asks why the Patriarch, who is the strongest man any of them know, still bows to a Sect deacon half his age, Uncle Mao sets down his cane and draws a ladder in the dust with its tip.

"Nine rungs of Qi Refining," he says, tapping the bottom of it. "First to third, you learn to hold Qi at all. You can light a Fire Starter, carry a Mirror Guard, feel a beast before you see it. Fourth to sixth, your channels are wide enough for true spells. Lin Feng's ring of fire, Wenshi's sword arc. Seventh to ninth, you can cast without hand seals and keep it up long enough to win a fight." He draws a thick line above the ninth rung. "Then Foundation Establishment. Your Qi stops being mist and becomes something solid. Flight. A spiritual sense you can throw across a valley. Two hundred and fifty years of life instead of a hundred and twenty. That is the Deacon. That is the Zhao Patriarch." Above the line he draws more rungs, faster, carelessly. "Then Purple Mansion. Golden Core. Nascent Soul. Above that, nobody in this county has ever seen one, so you may consider them stories."

"And the things we use?" asks Lin Shu, a thin, quiet side-branch cousin.

"Graded the same way, and each rank or grade splits again into four tiers: low, medium, high and peak. Low matches the first three rungs, medium the middle three, high the seventh and eighth, and peak the ninth. A low-tier pill is for a low-tier cultivator. A peak-tier beast is a match for a ninth-rung man. Mortal grade is what a farmer can hold: Fourth Uncle's guard swords, your aunt's water slips. Yellow grade is ours, made for Qi Refining hands. Profound grade wants a Foundation." He shrugs. "Earth, Heaven and the rest you'll read about in books, and you'll be lucky to touch one in your lives. Pills go by number instead, one to nine. Your aunt's Breath-Gathering Pills are grade one, low tier. A Foundation Establishment Pill is grade three, and costs more than this house." He knocks the ladder flat with his cane. "Beasts by rank. A first-rank beast is a match for a Qi Refining cultivator, low tier to peak, rung for rung. Second rank, for a Foundation. If you ever meet a third-rank beast, you run. Your Uncle Wenyuan met one that was only half-grown, and you've all seen his arm."

The children are silent. Above them, in the roof tiles, Lin Jian files the ladder away next to the generating cycle and counts the rungs between himself and the top.

He also scans, when he can. Never more than once a day, and only things no one will miss. A rusted arrowhead dug out of the eastern terraces, which turns out to have been forged with Qi-infused charcoal by a technique the panel says no longer exists. A frog. A feather from the roof. Every one of them goes into the library in his head, and the Creation Energy creeps upward, one or two at a time.

```
Creation Energy: 31 / 100
```

He is careful. He is very, very careful. But once, when he is five, he looks down from his hollow in the roof tiles and finds Uncle Mao looking straight back up at him with the cane resting across his knees.

The old man says nothing. He goes back to his lesson. But after that, he begins to speak a little louder, and sometimes, when he says something important, he says it twice.

\ \ \*

The Root Stele lives in the ancestral hall and comes out only on testing days.

It is a black stone pillar as tall as a man, carved with the five symbols of the elements, and set into its face are five crystal resonators the size of hen's eggs. Gold for metal. Green for wood. Blue for water. Red for fire. Brown for earth. A child lays a palm on the plate at its base and pushes a breath of whatever is inside him into the stone, and the crystals answer. Bright for a strong root. Dim for a weak one. Dark for none.

Lin Jian is six. It is the spring after his birthday, and the whole family is in the ancestral hall for his testing. Not because anyone expects much, but because it is the custom, and because Grandfather insists on customs more and more as he gets older.

Lin Hu is there, eight now and broad and loud, at the second layer already. He leans toward Lin Feng and whispers loudly enough to be heard across the hall. "Radish is going to be a farmer."

Lin Feng, who is twelve and at the fourth layer and has not yet decided whether he loves or resents his small strange brother, says, "Shut up, Hu," without turning his head.

Grandfather nods. Lin Jian walks to the stele and lays his palm on the plate.

He has thought about this moment for three years. He has run every possible outcome. He knows the flicker on the Root-Seeking Jade. He knows roughly what is coming. He does not try to hide anything. There is no point; a stele cannot be fooled by a six-year-old, and he wants to see the truth as much as anyone.

And he wants the scan.

He pushes a breath into the stone. At the same moment, under cover of the test, he lets the blue line sweep.

The crystals light.

All five of them.

For a heartbeat the hall is quiet, and then it relaxes, because five lights is what most of the village children show. Then they look closer and the quiet changes. The lights are dim. Gold, green, blue, red, brown, each one no brighter than a coal at the bottom of a cold hearth. Each one flickering, as if the five are crowding one another for room.

Lin Hu laughs. His mother hushes him.

Grandfather looks at the stele for a long time. "A five-element root," he says at last, to the hall. His voice is steady. "Common as river stones, and as dull. All five elements, none of them strong. It will be slow. It is not nothing. Lin Jian may cultivate."

May. Everyone in the hall hears the word. A five-element root cultivates the way a loaded cart climbs a hill: it gets there, a long time after the others.

Lin Jian takes his hand off the plate and bows, as he has been taught. Across the hall he catches sight of his mother. She is not looking at him. She is looking at the stele, with her eyes narrowed, as if it has done something she did not expect.

Then the panel opens, and he stops paying attention to anything else.

```
[Scan: Elemental Resonance Stele]
Structure: Qi-conductive crystal channels, five tuned resonators, palm plate
Blueprint: Partial (64%)
Creation Energy +5 (36 / 100)

[Host Root Analysis — Reference Acquired]
Metal: 11% purity
Wood: 9% purity
Water: 13% purity
Fire: 8% purity
Earth: 10% purity
Integration: Poor (mutual interference)

Root Structure Analysis: 3%
```

And below that, a line he reads three times.

```
[Interference Analysis]
Estimated Qi absorption loss: 61%
Cause: Simultaneous multi-element intake. Resonance conflict during circulation.
Note: Loss is circulation-dependent, not structural.
Optimization possible.
```

Not structural.

The problem is not his root. The problem is the way everyone breathes.

\ \ \*

That evening his father finds him on the eastern wall, sitting with his knees drawn up, looking at nothing.

Lin Wenyuan sits down beside him with a grunt. For a while neither of them says anything.

"When I was thirty-four," his father says at last, "a shadow lynx came down out of the mountains while I was walking the north terraces. I never saw it. I felt the claw go in, here." He touches his left shoulder. "When I woke up, four of my primary channels were torn, and the healers said they would never mend. I had been at the fifth layer and rising fast. Everyone said I would be the next Patriarch." He smiles a little. "I sat on this wall for a month."

Lin Jian looks at him.

"Your grandfather came up one morning and put a talisman brush in my hand," his father says. "He said, a man who can't hold a sword can still hold a pen. I thought he was mocking me. He wasn't. Half the stones in this family's treasury come from that brush now." He looks down at his son. "The stele measures what you were given, Jian. It doesn't measure what you'll make of it. Remember that."

"I will," says Lin Jian.

He does. He also remembers, as his father gets up stiffly and goes back down the steps, that the healers said the channels would never mend, and that his panel has just told him a problem everyone in this world believes is fixed by birth is nothing of the kind.

He goes to bed thinking about gates.

\ \ \*

His first lesson comes nine days later.

Uncle Mao meets him in the courtyard at dawn, alone, which is not usual. The old man looks at him for a while without saying anything, leaning on his cane.

"Lin Feng sensed Qi on his third day," he says. "Lin Hu, in a month. A five-element root, I'm told, can take half a year. Sometimes they never manage it at all, and after a year we send them to the rice fields and they live a good life and die at seventy." He lowers himself onto the bench. "Sit. You know how to sit; I've watched you do it on my storehouse roof for two years."

Lin Jian sits.

"The sensing breath," says Uncle Mao. "In for eight. Hold for four. Out for eight. Draw it down to here, below your navel. Don't push. Don't grab. Just breathe, and listen for something that isn't air."

Lin Jian closes his eyes and breathes.

He feels it on the first breath.

He has felt it for years, really, as pressure around people, as warmth off stones. But now, with his breath slow and his attention turned inward, it comes into him like a draft into a cold house. A thin, cool, tingling stream, entering through his skin and his lungs together. And immediately, he feels it go wrong. The stream comes in tangled, five threads twisting around one another, and where they cross they grind. Like gears with mismatched teeth. Most of it scatters before it ever reaches his belly.

He opens his eyes.

Uncle Mao is watching him with his mouth slightly open.

"Well?" the old man says.

There is no point pretending he felt nothing. Uncle Mao has been teaching children for twenty years; he would know. "Something cold," Lin Jian says. "It comes in. But it falls apart."

Uncle Mao says nothing for a long moment. "First breath," he says at last, quietly, to himself. Then, louder: "Good. Keep doing that. Every morning and every night. Don't tell your brother; he'll sulk for a month."

A new frame unfolds in Lin Jian's vision as he walks away.

```
[Host Monitoring (Limited)]
Qi intake (per cycle): 0.0031
Interference loss: 61%
Qi reaching dantian: 4%
```

Four percent. He breathes in a river and keeps a cup.

\ \ \*

He works on it at night, lying on his back in the dark beside his sleeping brother, running experiments the way he used to run them in a lab.

Water alone, if he can find it in the tangle and let the others go: three percent. Worse. A single element at thirteen percent purity simply is not enough to carry anything. Water and wood together, the pair the cycle says feed one another: six percent. Better. The two threads do not grind. They slide together, one into the other.

So the cycle is real. It is a resonance chain.

Then he does the obvious thing, which nobody in ten thousand years has had any reason to try, because nobody with a root strong enough to cultivate has ever needed it. He opens one gate at a time.

Water on the first breath, and only water. Wood on the second, while the water is still moving, so that the water feeds it. Fire on the third. Earth on the fourth. Metal on the fifth. Then water again, riding the metal. Around and around, one element per breath, never two at once, like a five-stroke engine turning over.

The first night he manages it for perhaps a dozen breaths before he loses the rhythm. The panel blinks.

```
Qi reaching dantian: 11%
```

Eleven. Nearly three times the standard method.

He calls it the Five-Gate Wheel. Not out loud. Never out loud.

Within a week it is fourteen percent. Within two, seventeen. The tangle in his channels smooths out like a combed rope. The cold thread runs down into his belly and pools there, a little more each night, and stays.

On the nineteenth night, he is so deep in the rhythm that he does not hear the door.

"How long have you been doing this?"

He opens his eyes. His mother is sitting on the floor by the door with her back against the wall, her knees drawn up, watching him in the moonlight from the window. He does not know how long she has been there. Long enough.

He thinks about lying. He has thought, many times, about what he will say when someone finally catches him. But his mother is not someone you lie to by accident. She spent ten years among men who lied for a living, and she is still alive.

"Since the first lesson," he says.

"And what are you doing?"

He chooses his words with great care. "I let it in a little at a time," he says. "One kind at a time. If they all come at once, they fight."

His mother says nothing for a long while.

"When I was a rogue," she says at last, "I knew a man in the Eastern Sea with a four-element root. Everyone told him he'd never pass the third layer. He built his own breathing method. Spent ten years on it. He reached the eighth layer by forty." She looks at the moonlit floor between them. "A sect elder heard about the method. They offered to buy it. He refused. They found him a month later in a ditch with his dantian crushed. The method was never found."

Lin Jian sits very still.

"There was a boy, too," she says. "In an eastern sect. Five elements, like you. Someone gave him a good method and he pushed too fast and his channels burst. Two years, and he was dead." She looks at him. "Both of those things can happen to you. Do you understand me?"

"Yes, Mother."

"Good." She gets up. "Then here is what we'll do. I won't ask you how you thought of it. I won't tell anyone, not your father, not your grandfather. But from now on, when you cultivate at night, I sit by the door. And when you reach the first layer, you tell no one. Not Uncle Mao. Not your brother. Let them think it takes you a year."

"Yes, Mother."

She stops at the door. "One more thing. I am a fourth-layer cultivator, and every cultivator in this house believes I am a third. Do you know why?" He shakes his head. "Because I fold my Qi the way you fold a letter. It is called the Still Water Veil. A stranger's sense reads the fold and not the letter. It will hide a layer or two from anyone near your own strength, and a beast's nose will pass over you if you are quiet and the wind is right. Folded all the way, a first-layer cultivator reads as a mortal child. It will not hide you from anyone whose Qi runs much deeper than yours. Your grandfather sees through mine as through a window."

She shows him: the fold, the breath, the hold. It takes him eleven days. On the twelfth she walks through the room twice with her eyes open, looks straight at the corner where he sits, and does not find him.

"Again tomorrow," she says.

She ruffles his hair once, very lightly, and goes back to bed.

\ \ \*

He reaches the first layer of Qi Refining on the twenty-first night.

It does not feel like much. A warmth below his navel that does not fade when he stops breathing the wheel. A grain of something, no bigger than a mustard seed, that holds the cold thread and does not let it go. The channels to his hands open, one after the other, like doors in a long corridor, and a tingling runs down his arms and into his fingertips.

Lin Feng took four months. Lin Hu took nearly five.

Across the room, by the door, his mother opens her eyes and looks at him. Neither of them says anything. She nods once, and closes her eyes again.

The panel opens in front of him, and keeps opening.

```
[Host Status Update]
Qi Sensing: Complete
Energy Channels: Opened (hands, 2 / 2)
Host Qi Reserve: 0.62 (Qi Refining, Layer 1)

[Energy Source Detected: Host Qi]
Fabrication Module: ONLINE
```

The words sit there in the dark, blue and steady, and Lin Jian reads them again, and again, and once more to be sure.

```
ARK-7 Fabrication Interface — Level 1
Scan Module: Online
Fabrication Module: Online (Limited: Host Qi only)
Blueprint Library: 44 entries available
Locked: living material, spirit-grade material, all Level 2+ items
```

He opens the library and scrolls. The hemp cloth. The rice. The arrowhead. The candied ginger. Most of them are useless. A few are not. One stops him cold: a blueprint the interface has built quietly out of three separate scans, a sliver of white willow bark he once chewed on the riverbank, a cup of water, and one of Third Aunt's charcoal-bitter pills.

```
[Blueprint: Willow Bark Extract]
Class: Salicylate analgesic, anti-inflammatory
Inputs: inner bark of white willow (approx. 1 jin), clean water
Required Qi: 0.80
Status: Available
```

Across the room his father, who has come in late from his desk to look in on his sons as he does every night, stands in the doorway for a moment, rubbing his left shoulder with his good hand in the slow, absent way of a man who has been in pain so long he no longer notices it.

Then he goes out, and the door closes softly behind him.

Lin Jian lies back down, closes his eyes, and begins the wheel again, because he is eighteen hundredths of a point of Qi short of what he needs.

Three, he thinks. Fix Father.
